description: We are a multidisciplinary team from the IEEE Student Branch at École Mohammadia d’Ingénieurs (EMI), passionate about AI, software development, robotics, data science, and space exploration. We enjoy turning complex problems into creative, practical solutions and are excited to collaborate on challenges that have a real-world impact.
summary:
AstroHealth AI is a health console for astronauts on long missions, built and tested around a Mars surface simulation. A chest sensor streams ECG data and other biosignals, and an AI service measures heart rate, heart-rate variability and beat type, and flags anything that needs the medical officer. Crew also get an interactive anatomy view, orthostatic and stress tests, and a camera-based exercise coach that counts good reps to protect bone and muscle. ORBI, a voice-activated companion, briefs the crew, guides their daily mission plan and awards XP, ranks and streaks to keep them motivated. Mission control manages crew accounts and plans.

On Mars, a message to a flight surgeon can take 22 minutes each way, so crew must monitor their own health. AstroHealth AI gives them clear, explainable guidance when data is uncertain, and it says so instead of guessing. This matters because early detection of cardiac, musculoskeletal and stress problems protects both crew safety and mission success. It is a research prototype, not a medical device.
details:
AstroHealth AI is a crew health console for long-duration missions, built around a Mars surface simulation. A Python AI service takes the ECG signal, cleans it, finds the heartbeats, and works out heart rate, heart-rate variability and a beat classification. It also rates signal quality, and when the signal is poor it reports “inconclusive” instead of guessing. Open alerts appear on the crew console.

Beyond the ECG, crew get:

  • an interactive 3D body and anatomy view, with a page for each body area (brain, lungs, spine, arms and others);
  • orthostatic and exercise stress tests that work out a risk estimate from the heart-rate response;
  • a camera-based exercise coach (MediaPipe pose tracking) that counts good reps, including a mode adapted for resistive exercise devices on a spacecraft;
  • a daily mission plan with XP, ranks and streaks;
  • ORBI, a voice-activated companion who briefs crew and guides the day.

Benefits and intended impact. On Mars a message to a flight surgeon can take about 22 minutes each way, so crew must monitor their own health. The app gives them clear, explainable guidance, keeps data private to each crew member, and helps protect heart, bone and muscle health and mental readiness. It is a research prototype and not a medical device.

Tools and technology.

  • Frontend: Angular 18 and TypeScript, WebSockets (STOMP), MediaPipe in the browser.
  • Backend: Java 21, Spring Boot 3, Spring Security with JWT login, PostgreSQL, Flyway.
  • AI service: Python, FastAPI, scikit-learn, with a beat classifier using standard (AAMI) beat classes.
  • Hardware: ESP32 with an AD8232 ECG module.
  • Hosting: Vercel for the frontend and Railway for the backend, the AI service and the database.

Creativity. The app turns health monitoring into a mission companion, with a robot, daily tasks and progress rewards that keep crew engaged. It stays honest about uncertainty, and it runs without the hardware through a demo mode with a synthetic ECG.

Factors the team considered. Privacy, so admins can’t see raw heart data. Safety, so the app says “inconclusive” rather than guess. Working with no connection to Earth. Crew motivation. Not claiming clinical validity.
